subject: Biology
title: Homeostasis (KPK Board)
learningOutcomes: Define homeostasis and describe its importance; define osmoregulation, excretion and thermoregulation.
Explain osmotic adjustments in mesophytes, hydrophytes, xerophytes and halophytes.
Describe the mechanisms and adaptations in plants for the excretion and storage of carbon dioxide, water, oxygen, latex, resins and gums.
State the skin, lungs and kidneys as the major organs of homeostasis and describe how the lungs keep the carbon dioxide concentration down to a certain level.
Explain the role of the skin in regulating body temperature.
Explain that the kidneys control the composition of blood.
Identify the different organs of the urinary system.
Relate the structure of the kidney to its function; state that the nephron is the functional unit and locate the parts of a nephron with their functions.
State that the main role of the kidney is urine formation and describe pressure filtration, reabsorption and tubular secretion.
Explain that the kidney plays an important role in osmoregulation.
Identify the causes of kidney stones and name surgery and lithotripsy as the methods of removing them.
Outline the causes of kidney failure and describe dialysis (haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis) and kidney transplantation as its treatments.
Describe the contributions of Al-Farabi and Abul-Qasim in introducing the method of removing stones from the urinary bladder.

sections.heading: Homeostasis and the Internal Environment
sections.body: Living organisms have evolved and adapted according to their environment, but the conditions of the external environment keep on changing, and these changes affect the internal environment as well. Organisms overcome the effect of these changes by making adjustments inside their bodies so that the internal environment stays constant or nearly constant. This ability is called homeostasis, and it helps an organism to survive and to utilise its environment in the best possible way. The terms internal environment and external environment were coined by Claude Bernard a century ago. The components of the internal environment most readily affected by fluctuations outside are water, solutes and temperature.

sections.heading: Osmoregulation, Excretion and Thermoregulation
sections.body: Body fluids are made up of water and solutes, and the water-solute balance (commonly called the water-salt balance) is very important. The process by which the amount of water and solutes is maintained in the body is called osmoregulation. Excretion is the elimination of harmful solutes (for example nitrogenous wastes) and extra water from the body. All metabolic reactions are catalysed by enzymes and each enzyme works best at a suitable body temperature, so organisms keep their internal temperature within a tolerable range; this is called thermoregulation. Osmoregulation, excretion and thermoregulation are all parts of homeostasis.

sections.heading: Osmoregulation in Plants
sections.body: On the basis of the availability of water, plants are divided into four groups. Mesophytes live on land where enough water is available; they absorb water through the roots, keep the stomata open when water is plentiful, close them in a shortage and have a waxy cuticle (maize, clover, rose). Hydrophytes live in freshwater or wet soil; water enters through their whole surface, so many have broad floating leaves with many stomata on the upper surface (water lily). Xerophytes live in dry places such as deserts; they have deep roots, very few stomata, a thick waxy cuticle and succulent stems or roots that store water (cacti). Halophytes live in salty water; they absorb salts by active transport so that water does not leave their cells, and store extra salt or excrete it from salt glands on the leaves (sea grasses).

sections.heading: Excretion in Plants
sections.body: Plants do not possess any special organs for excretion. By day, carbon dioxide is retained in the leaves for photosynthesis and the extra oxygen is released through the stomata; at night, when there is no photosynthesis, carbon dioxide is excreted through the open stomata. Extra water, stored in the vacuoles to give turgor, is removed by transpiration (stomatal, cuticular and lenticular) during the day and by guttation at night, when little drops of water come out of small pores at the tips or edges of the leaves, as in grasses. Other wastes are stored as harmless crystals, lost with falling leaves, or excreted through special pores: latex by the rubber plant, gums by the Acacia tree, resins by coniferous trees and mucilage by the ladyfinger.

sections.heading: Lungs, Skin and Thermoregulation
sections.body: In human beings the main organs of homeostasis are the skin, lungs and kidneys. Cellular respiration produces carbon dioxide, an acidic gas that would make the blood and body tissues more acidic if it accumulated. Blood carries it to the lungs, where it diffuses into the air in the alveoli and is exhaled. The skin of mammals is the organ of thermoregulation: a thin layer of fat cells beneath the epidermis does not allow heat to enter or leave the body. In cold conditions the muscles at the base of the hairs contract, the hairs stand up and goose bumps form, making a blanket of warm air. In warm conditions the sweat glands produce sweat, and its evaporation cools the body and also removes some water, salts and nitrogenous wastes.

sections.heading: Kidneys and the Liver
sections.body: The kidneys are the most important organs of homeostasis. They filter the nitrogenous wastes from the blood and excrete them, and they control the water-solute balance: if there are more solutes in the blood they excrete them and retain water, and if there is more water they produce more urine to remove the excess. In this way the kidneys perform osmoregulation. The liver also plays a role: it breaks down the haemoglobin of dead red blood cells (the products go to the kidneys for removal) and changes ammonia, produced in the metabolism of proteins, into urea, which the kidneys then remove.

sections.heading: The Urinary System
sections.body: The human urinary system (excretory system) consists of a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra. The kidneys remove extra water, salts and nitrogenous wastes from the blood and produce urine. From each kidney a tube called the ureter carries urine to the urinary bladder, which temporarily stores it. The urethra is the tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body.

sections.heading: Structure of the Kidney
sections.body: The two bean-shaped, dark brown kidneys lie below the diaphragm in the abdominal cavity, on the sides of the vertebral column and attached to the dorsal body wall; the right kidney is slightly lower and smaller. Each is about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 4 cm thick, and together they weigh less than 1% of the body weight yet receive 20% of the blood supplied with each heartbeat. A renal capsule encloses the kidney; the hilus on the concave side is where the renal artery enters and the renal vein and ureter leave. A longitudinal section shows an outer renal cortex and an inner renal medulla with cone-shaped renal pyramids, whose tips lie in the renal pelvis that extends outside to form the ureter.

sections.heading: The Nephron
sections.body: The functional units of the kidneys are the nephrons, more than one million in each kidney. A nephron has a renal corpuscle and a renal tubule. The renal corpuscle is the first part and is made of the glomerulus (a network of capillaries) and the cup-shaped Bowman's capsule around it. The renal tubule is a long tube with three parts: the convoluted proximal convoluted tubule, the U-shaped Loop of Henle and the convoluted distal convoluted tubule. The distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons open into a single collecting duct, and many collecting ducts open into the renal pelvis.

sections.heading: Urine Formation
sections.body: The main role of the kidney is urine formation, which has three sub-processes. In pressure filtration, the high pressure of blood in the glomerulus filters water, salts, sugars and nitrogenous wastes into the Bowman's capsule as glomerular filtrate; blood cells and plasma proteins stay behind because they are larger. In reabsorption, the useful constituents are taken back into the blood capillaries around the renal tubule: some water and most of the glucose in the proximal convoluted tubule, salts in the Loop of Henle and most of the water in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. In tubular secretion, wastes such as salts, hydrogen ions and urea are added from the capillaries to the tubule. The filtrate is then urine, which passes through the renal pelvis, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra.

sections.heading: Osmoregulation and the Kidneys
sections.body: The kidneys mainly perform osmoregulatory and excretory functions. When body fluids and blood have a limited amount of water, more water is reabsorbed from the glomerular filtrate into the blood capillaries, so the volume of urine decreases and water is conserved. When there is an excess of water, the reabsorption of water is reduced, more water remains in the renal tubule and more urine is produced, so the excess water is released. The kidney conserves water by reabsorbing over 99.5% of the glomerular filtrate, and human kidneys start functioning right after the fourth month of gestation.

sections.heading: Kidney Disorders and Kidney Stones
sections.body: High sugar in the blood in diabetes damages the blood vessels that filter the blood in the kidneys, which can lead to weight gain, ankle swelling and more proteins in the urine. Kidney stones form when filtered harmful substances (calcium oxalate, calcium and ammonium phosphate, uric acid) gather in the kidneys and make larger objects that cannot pass in the urine. Causes include a diet rich in these substances (green vegetables, fats, dairy products), extra vitamins C and D, reduced water intake, excess uric acid, urinary tract infections and alcohol. Small stones are passed by drinking plenty of water, large stones need surgery, and lithotripsy uses shock-waves to break the stones into tiny pieces that leave in the urine.

sections.heading: Kidney Failure, Dialysis and Transplantation
sections.body: In kidney (renal) failure the nephrons are progressively destroyed, so the blood is not filtered properly and the level of urea and other nitrogenous wastes rises. The most common causes are long-term diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Dialysis is the artificial cleaning of the blood: in haemodialysis blood flows inside the semi-permeable tubes of a dialyzer while dialysis fluid flows outside; in peritoneal dialysis dialysis fluid is filled into the peritoneal cavity through a catheter, wastes diffuse into it from the blood vessels of the peritoneum and it is drained later, and this can be done at home. Kidney transplantation, the advanced treatment, places a healthy kidney from a deceased or living donor in the patient, matched with the patient's immune system.

sections.heading: Contributions of Muslim Scientists
sections.body: Abul-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936–1013 AD), known in the west as Abulcasis, is best known for his breakthrough in surgery; his thirty-volume Medical Encyclopedia, Al-Tasrif, describes operations he performed, including the removal of stone from the urinary bladder. Abu Nasr Al-Farabi (Alpharabius, 872–950 AD), the great Turkish philosopher and scientist, wrote many books and gave a lot of information about kidney diseases, including stones in the urinary bladder. Abu Bakar Muhammad ibn Zakariya Al Razi, born in 865 AD in Persia, introduced techniques to remove kidney stones, and his book The Book of Formation of Small Stones was acclaimed all over the world.

definitions.definition: The ability to maintain the internal environment constant or nearly constant.
The process by which the amount of water and solutes is maintained in the body.
The elimination of harmful solutes (e.g. nitrogenous wastes) and extra water from the body.
The maintenance of the internal body temperature within a tolerable range.
Terrestrial plants which live where a sufficient quantity of water is available, e.g. maize, clover and rose.
Plants which live in freshwater or in wet soil, e.g. the water lily.
Plants which live in dry environments such as deserts, e.g. cacti.
Plants which live in habitats with salty waters, e.g. sea grasses.
The loss of water from the plant surface in the form of vapours.
The removal of extra water as little drops from small pores at the tips or edges of leaves, mostly at night.
Bumps on the skin formed when the muscles at the base of the hairs contract in cold conditions.
An increase in body temperature when the set point of the hypothalamus is displaced above the normal 37 °C during infection.
The functional unit of the kidney, made of a renal corpuscle and a renal tubule.
The first part of the nephron, composed of the glomerulus and the Bowman's capsule.
A network of capillaries inside the Bowman's capsule.
The cup-shaped structure around the glomerulus.
The long tube attached to the Bowman's capsule: proximal convoluted tubule, Loop of Henle and distal convoluted tubule.
The material filtered from the glomerulus and collected in the Bowman's capsule.
Filtration of water, salts, sugars and nitrogenous wastes from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule due to high blood pressure.
The return of useful constituents of the filtrate from the renal tubule into the blood capillaries.
The addition of waste materials such as salts, hydrogen ions and urea from the blood capillaries to the renal tubule.
The filtrate present in the renal tubule after pressure filtration, reabsorption and tubular secretion.
Larger objects formed when harmful filtered substances gather in the kidneys; they cannot pass in the urine.
The most recent, non-surgical removal of kidney stones by shock-waves that break them into tiny pieces.
The condition in which the nephrons are progressively destroyed and stop functioning.
The cleaning of the blood of a patient with renal failure by artificial methods.
Dialysis in which blood is passed through a dialyzer containing semi-permeable tubes.
Dialysis in which dialysis fluid is filled in the peritoneal cavity through a catheter; it can be done at home.
The advanced treatment of kidney failure in which a healthy kidney from a donor is placed in the patient.

examTips: Learn the four terms together: homeostasis (keeping the internal environment constant), osmoregulation (water and solutes), excretion (harmful solutes and extra water) and thermoregulation (temperature).

Prepare the four plant groups as a table: mesophytes (medium water, waxy cuticle), hydrophytes (freshwater, floating leaves with stomata on the upper surface), xerophytes (deep roots, few stomata, succulent stems) and halophytes (salty water, active transport of salts, salt glands).
Differentiate transpiration (vapours, by day, through stomata, cuticle and lenticels) from guttation (little drops, at night, from pores at the tips or edges of leaves).
Learn the nephron in order: renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule) → proximal convoluted tubule → Loop of Henle → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct → renal pelvis.

Remember urine formation as three steps: pressure filtration (glomerulus), reabsorption (water and glucose back to the blood) and tubular secretion (wastes added to the tubule). Glomerular filtrate is not urine.
Know the difference between the two dialysis methods (dialyzer vs peritoneal cavity and catheter) and that only peritoneal dialysis is stated to be done at home.

interactiveLesson.instructions: Explore each labelled part of the nephron (Fig. 11.10). Select every hotspot to continue.

hotspots.label: Renal Corpuscle
hotspots.fact: The first part of the nephron, made of the glomerulus and the Bowman's capsule.

hotspots.label: Glomerulus
hotspots.fact: A network of capillaries where the high blood pressure filters water, salts, sugars and nitrogenous wastes.

hotspots.label: Bowman's Capsule
hotspots.fact: The cup-shaped structure around the glomerulus that collects the glomerular filtrate.

hotspots.label: Arteriole
hotspots.fact: A branch of the renal artery that divides further into the capillaries of the glomerulus.

hotspots.label: Blood Capillaries
hotspots.fact: They surround the renal tubule and take back the useful constituents of the filtrate during reabsorption.

hotspots.label: Proximal Convoluted Tubule
hotspots.fact: The first, convoluted part of the renal tubule; some water and most of the glucose are reabsorbed here.

hotspots.label: Loop of Henle
hotspots.fact: The U-shaped middle part of the renal tubule, where salts are reabsorbed.

hotspots.label: Distal Convoluted Tubule
hotspots.fact: The last, convoluted part of the renal tubule; most of the water is reabsorbed here.

hotspots.label: Collecting Duct
hotspots.fact: Receives the distal convoluted tubules of many nephrons; many collecting ducts open into the renal pelvis.

hotspots.label: Towards the Ureter
hotspots.fact: Urine goes from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder through the ureter.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The ability to maintain the internal environment constant is called:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Maintaining the internal environment constant or nearly constant is called homeostasis.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which group of plants stores water in soft and juicy succulent stems or roots?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Some xerophytes, such as cacti, store water in succulent stems or roots.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Grasses remove extra water at night through small pores at the tips of their leaves. This process is called:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Transpiration does not occur at night, so grasses remove extra water as little drops by guttation.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The functional unit of the kidney is the:
practiceQuestions.explanation: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney; each kidney has more than one million of them.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In which structure does pressure filtration of the blood take place?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The high pressure of blood in the glomerulus filters water, salts, sugars and nitrogenous wastes into the Bowman's capsule.

practiceQuestions.prompt: From which part of the nephron is most of the glucose reabsorbed?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Some water and most of the glucose are reabsorbed from the proximal convoluted tubule.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The most recent non-surgical method of removing kidney stones is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Lithotripsy uses shock-waves to break kidney stones into tiny pieces that pass out in the urine.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which form of dialysis can be done at home?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In peritoneal dialysis, the dialysis fluid is filled in the peritoneal cavity through a catheter and later drained; this form can be done at home.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Halophytes absorb salts from the external water by active transport so that water does not move out of their cells.
practiceQuestions.explanation: By absorbing salts by active transport, halophytes keep water from moving out of their cells.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Glomerular filtrate and urine are exactly the same.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The filtrate becomes urine only after reabsorption and tubular secretion in the renal tubule.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The urethra carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The ureter carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder; the urethra carries it from the bladder to the outside.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In cold conditions, the muscles at the base of the hair contract, the hairs stand up and goose bumps form.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The hair and goose bumps make a blanket of warm air that does not allow body heat to go out.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The tube that carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside is the ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The urethra carries urine from the urinary bladder to the outside of the body.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Each kidney contains more than one ____ nephrons.
practiceQuestions.explanation: There are more than one million nephrons in each kidney.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Abul-Qasim al-Zahrawi is known in the west as ____.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Abul-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936–1013 AD) is known in the west as Abulcasis.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the parts in the order through which the filtrate passes from the Bowman's capsule to the ureter.
sequencingActivity.explanation: The filtrate collected in the Bowman's capsule passes through the proximal convoluted tubule, Loop of Henle and distal convoluted tubule into the collecting duct, then to the renal pelvis and the ureter.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A person has sweated heavily in hot weather and drunk very little water. Which change is expected in the kidneys?

options: Less water is reabsorbed, so more urine is produced
More water is reabsorbed, so less urine is produced
More water is reabsorbed, so more urine is produced
Water is not reabsorbed at all

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: When the body has a limited amount of water, more water is reabsorbed from the glomerular filtrate into the blood capillaries, so the volume of urine decreases and water is conserved.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Blood cells and plasma proteins are found in the fluid collected in a patient's Bowman's capsule. What does this suggest?

options: The filtration is not normal, because blood cells and plasma proteins are normally too large to be filtered
Everything is normal, because all blood components are filtered
The patient has a kidney stone in the ureter
Tubular secretion has added the cells to the filtrate

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: In pressure filtration only water, salts, sugars and nitrogenous wastes are filtered; blood cells and plasma proteins are not filtered out because they are larger in size.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A patient with kidney failure wants a treatment that can be done at home, without a machine such as a dialyzer. According to the chapter, which treatment fits?
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: In peritoneal dialysis the dialysis fluid is filled in the peritoneal cavity through a catheter, wastes diffuse into it and the fluid is drained later; this form can be done at home.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: In tubular secretion, wastes such as hydrogen ions and urea move from the blood capillaries into the renal ______.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Tubular secretion adds waste materials from the blood capillaries to the renal tubule.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Most of the water in the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Most of the water is reabsorbed from the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting duct; the proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs some water and most of the glucose.
